I have farmed these fields in Quzhou for over fifty years. I never went to school, but I know this soil better than any book. I have four mu of good flat land here on the North China Plain. This year, like every year, I will grow winter wheat and summer maize in rotation — it is the only system I trust, and at my age I do not gamble with new crops.

My wheat is already in the ground from last October, waking up now with the spring warmth. I used my usual improved wheat seed from the county supply shop — not the most expensive kind, but the kind that has done right by me for years. Last autumn I rotary-tilled the land and put down about 100 jin of compound fertilizer per mu as basal dressing. Now that the season has started, I will topdress with urea when the wheat joints, and I will irrigate four times through spring: once now as it greens up, once at jointing, once at heading, and once more if the weather turns dry. I will spray for insects twice, lay down herbicide once, and use fungicide once when the humidity rises. I expect around 1,050 jin per mu if the weather is fair.

In early June, the day the wheat turns golden, I will harvest it immediately. I will not plough the field — there is no time, and the straw will be chopped and left on the soil to protect it. That same week I will plant hybrid maize seed, the kind with big ears that the shop recommends. I will put down another 100 jin of compound fertilizer per mu and topdress with urea when the corn is knee-high. Maize needs two good irrigations: one when the leaves are wrapping, and one when the tassels emerge. I will spray three times for pests and weeds. If the summer rains come on time, I should get 1,150 jin per mu of corn.

I am sixty-eight. My back is not what it was, so I keep things simple. Wheat and corn have fed my family every single year, and they will feed us again.
